jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 4 on the unity of theology as a science, cross-referencing Aquinas, ST I q.1 a.3.

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e115.summary: Transition from the scientific status of theology to its unity, and first argument that it is one: Wisdom 10 speaks of 'the science of the saints' in the singular, apparently meaning theology.
claims: Scripture speaks of theology as one science (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e131.summary: Two further arguments for unity: whatever shares one formal ratio of knowability belongs to one habit, and everything theology treats shares the ratio of the revealable; and whatever is attributed to one principal subject belongs to one science, and all in theology is attributed to God.
claims: All of theology's contents share the ratio of the revealable (objection)
All of theology's contents are attributed to God as principal subject (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e156.summary: Contrary argument: the supernatural should mirror the natural, and creator and creatures, speculative and practical matters, known by natural reason belong to diverse sciences, so known by revelation they too belong to diverse sciences. Response: setting aside whether theology is strictly science and calling every theological cognitive habit 'science' in Augustine's broad sense, theology is not one science but several, because habits are distinguished both by objects and, more formally, by middles—as science and opinion of the same conclusion differ by necessary versus contingent middle. Habits are needed for the mode in which a power tends to its object, so habits differ formally by mode of tending (understanding of principles vs. discursive knowledge of conclusions; with or without fear); sciences differ among themselves only by objects, more like integral parts of a whole than species of a genus—offered as a speculative suggestion.
claims: Theology, taking 'science' broadly, is not one science but several
Cognitive habits are distinguished by objects and, more formally, by middles
Habits are distinguished formally by the power's mode of tending to its object
Distinction among proper sciences resembles that of parts of a whole more than species of a genus

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e265.summary: Applies the principle: theology in Q1's three senses—assent to Scripture (identical with faith), the defensive habit, and the habit of practical deduction from the articles—concerns diverse objects or proceeds by diverse middles, as will appear when the subject of theology is discussed; so it is several habits.
claims: The three theological habits differ by object or by middle, so theology is several habits

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e294.summary: Adds a further ground of distinction: the first habit (faith) is infused while the other two are acquired, and these two differ because in the defensive habit the articles function as conclusions, while in the deductive habit they function as principles.
claims: Faith is infused while the defensive and deductive habits are acquired
The articles are conclusions in the defensive habit and principles in the deductive habit

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e312.summary: Objection: even if theology includes three habits, it could still be one science, since one science involves several habits—of the principles and of the many conclusions corresponding to the subject's many properties.
claims: Objection: a single science includes many habits of principles and conclusions
concepts: unity of science and plurality of habits

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e334.summary: Rejects the objection: several habits may concur with one science extrinsically (antecedently, like the habit of principles, or concomitantly, like an opinative habit), but cannot belong to it intrinsically, since a superior notion cannot be multiplied within the nature of one inferior (as many animals cannot belong to one man's nature); habit is superior to science. And here, with 'science' taken broadly for any cognitive habit, unity of science is simply unity of habit.
claims: Several habits can concur with one science only extrinsically, not intrinsically
A higher genus cannot be multiplied within the essence of one of its inferiors
In the broad sense used here, science and cognitive habit are the same
concepts: intrinsic vs. extrinsic concurrence of habits

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e382.summary: Reply to the first argument: Wisdom 10 speaks only of the knowledge of faith sufficient for holy living, whereas theology has several senses; Scripture's singular wording is not meant to settle the unity of theological science, as Wisdom 7 enumerates gifts belonging to many sciences, and we call someone 'of great science' who has several sciences.
claims: Scripture's singular 'science of the saints' refers to the knowledge of faith and does not determine theology's unity

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e414.summary: Reply to the second argument: a common ratio of knowability can come from the object, by predication (as 'mobile' unifies physics, though not for proper properties) or by attribution (the third argument's case), or from the mode or middle of knowing. The 'revealable' is of the last kind—knowable on another's word or authority—and does not unify a habit; otherwise all things known by demonstration would form one science and all known dialectically one opinion.
claims: A common ratio of knowability may arise from predication, attribution, or mode of knowing
Being revealable means being knowable through authority
Sharing the ratio of the revealable does not make theology one habit

jsnvu6-d1e121-d1e482.summary: Reply to the third argument: attribution to a subject places things in the same science as the subject, but God is the subject only of theology in the second (defensive) sense; in the first and third senses the subject is the meritorious work, yet these differ as habits because they proceed by different middles, divine authority and human persuasion.
claims: God is the subject only of defensive theology
The subject of theology in the first and third senses is the meritorious work
Habits with the same subject but different middles are distinct

jsnvu6-d1e121.summary: Question 4 asks whether theology is one science. Taking 'science' broadly for any theological cognitive habit, Durandus answers that theology is several habits, not one. Cognitive habits are distinguished by objects and, more formally, by middles—since a habit concerns the mode in which a power tends to its object—so science and opinion of the same conclusion are distinct. The three senses of theology from Q1 (assent to Scripture, identical with infused faith; the acquired defensive habit, in which articles are conclusions; the acquired deductive habit, in which articles are principles) differ by object or by middle. He rejects the view that many habits can intrinsically compose one science, allowing only extrinsic concurrence. Replies: Scripture's singular 'science of the saints' concerns only faith; the 'revealable' is a ratio from the mode of knowing (authority) that cannot unify a habit; and God is the subject only of defensive theology, the subject of the first and third senses being the meritorious work, which they reach by different middles.
claims: Theology is not one science but several distinct cognitive habits
Cognitive habits are distinguished most formally by their middles
Several habits cannot intrinsically constitute one science
The ratio of the revealable does not unify theology
God is the subject only of theology as the defensive habit
